## Seven stages

::: {.stages}
| Stage | The complaint | What we build |
|:-:|---|---|
| 0 | (the baseline) | an agent with no memory |
| 1 | "You forgot what I said a second ago" | one thread: a list of messages |
| 2 | "I want separate conversations" | many threads: a dict of lists |
| 3 | "You forgot me when I started a new chat" | long-term memory: a `remember` tool + a prompt |
| 4 | "Now my roommate uses it too" | (no new code) the shared memory leaks |
| 5 | "Ben shouldn't see Ana's memories" | memory namespaced by user |
| 6 | "What do you actually know about me?" | one memory file per user, via the filesystem MCP server |
:::

::: {.why}
Each stage fixes the problem the last one exposed. Stages 2 and 5 end with the **framework version**.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Notebook: drafts/lesson1_8/memory_from_scratch.ipynb. Same order as the slides.
- The thread through the whole lesson: the model is stateless. "Memory" is always just what the app decides to send.
:::

```{.python}
%pip install -q -U "langchain>=1.4" langchain-google-genai

import os
from google.colab import userdata
os.environ["GOOGLE_API_KEY"] = userdata.get("GOOGLE_API_KEY")

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.messages import AIMessage, HumanMessage, SystemMessage, ToolMessage
from langchain.tools import tool

MODEL = "google_genai:gemini-flash-lite-latest"


def show(messages):
    """Print a list of messages the way the agent sees them."""
    for m in messages:
        m.pretty_print()
```

::: {.why}
`show()` is how we'll look at memory all lesson: **print the list the model actually receives.**
:::

## Stage 0: the code

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-7"}
agent = create_agent(MODEL, tools=[])

result = agent.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage("Hi, I'm Ana. I'm taking DS 250 and I prefer R over Python.")]})
show(result["messages"])

result = agent.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage("What's my name, and which language do I like?")]})
show(result["messages"])
```

::: {.why}
The second result holds **one** `HumanMessage` and **one** `AIMessage`. **The model is stateless:** whatever it "remembers" is whatever you send it.
:::

## Stage 1: by hand {.compact}

```{.python}
result = agent.invoke({
    "messages": [
        HumanMessage("Hi, I'm Ana. I'm taking DS 250 and I prefer R over Python."),
        AIMessage("Hi Ana! Nice to meet you. ... I'll make sure to provide R solutions ..."),
        HumanMessage("What's my name, and which language do I like?"),
    ]
})

show(result["messages"])
```

::: {.why}
It works: we pasted the first exchange back in. **But who wants to maintain that?**
:::

## Stage 1: save it as we go

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|4-9|5|6|7-8"}
thread = []


def chat(text):
    thread.append(HumanMessage(text))
    result = agent.invoke({"messages": thread})
    new_messages = result["messages"][len(thread):]   # what the agent added this turn
    thread.extend(new_messages)
    return thread[-1].text


print(chat("Hi, I'm Ana. I'm taking DS 250 and I prefer R over Python."))
print(chat("What's my name, and which language do I like?"))
```

::: {.why}
`show(thread)`: that list **is** the memory.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Why `[len(thread):]`? `invoke` returns our messages plus whatever it added (AI replies, and later, tool calls). We keep only the new ones.
:::


::: {.notes}
- Ana did homework, then came back the next day for her project and wanted a fresh chat.
- Three costs of one list: distraction (old material), tokens (resent every turn), and no way back to "just the homework."
- Fix: name each conversation. That name is the thread ID.
:::

## Stage 2: the problem, in code

```{.python}
# Ana's homework session
print(chat("Can you explain what a p-value is in one paragraph?"))
print(chat("Give me a quick example in R."))

# The next day: Ana means to start fresh on her project
print(chat("I'm starting my final project on bike-share ride data. What should I do first?"))
print(chat("Summarize what we've talked about in this conversation."))
```

::: {.why}
`len(thread)` keeps climbing. The "summary" covers the **homework too**.
:::

## Stage 2: a dict of lists

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|4-9|5"}
threads = {}


def chat(thread_id, text):
    history = threads.setdefault(thread_id, [])
    history.append(HumanMessage(text))
    result = agent.invoke({"messages": history})
    history.extend(result["messages"][len(history):])
    return history[-1].text


print(chat("homework", "Hi, I'm Ana. I'm taking DS 250 and I prefer R over Python."))
print(chat("homework", "Can you explain what a p-value is in one paragraph?"))
print(chat("project", "Summarize what we've talked about in this conversation."))
```

::: {.why}
Same `chat`, one new argument. The project summary only covers the project.
:::

## Framework version: checkpointer

```{=html}
<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 1100 300" role="img" aria-label="What we built maps to LangChain: the threads dict becomes InMemorySaver, the thread_id key becomes the thread_id in the config, and our append and extend become the checkpointer loading and saving.">
  <text class="dg-tag" x="40" y="30">WE BUILT</text>
  <text class="dg-tag" x="640" y="30">LANGCHAIN</text>

  <rect class="dg-box" x="40" y="50" width="420" height="60" rx="10" stroke="#30363d"/>
  <text class="dg-mono" x="62" y="88">threads = {}</text>
  <rect class="dg-box" x="640" y="50" width="420" height="60" rx="10" stroke="#7ee787"/>
  <text class="dg-mono" x="662" y="88" style="fill:#7ee787">checkpointer=InMemorySaver()</text>
  <line x1="470" y1="80" x2="630" y2="80" stroke="#8b949e" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>

  <rect class="dg-box" x="40" y="130" width="420" height="60" rx="10" stroke="#30363d"/>
  <text class="dg-mono" x="62" y="168">threads[thread_id]</text>
```

## Framework version: the code {.compact}

```{.python code-line-numbers="3|5-6|8-10|13"}
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

fw_agent = create_agent(MODEL, tools=[], checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

homework = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "homework"}}
project = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "project"}}

fw_agent.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage("Hi, I'm Ana. I prefer R over Python.")]}, homework)
fw_agent.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage("Which language do I like?")]}, homework)
fw_agent.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage("Which language do I like?")]}, project)

# The checkpointer's saved list for one thread: the same kind of list as threads["homework"] above
show(fw_agent.get_state(homework).values["messages"])
```

::: {.why}
We only send the **new** message now. The checkpointer does the `append` / `extend` we wrote by hand.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Some facts are about *Ana*, not about one conversation. They live outside every thread.
- Write: something has to decide a fact is worth keeping. We let the model decide.
- Read: saved facts must reach the model. We put them in the system prompt, every turn, every thread.
:::

## Stage 3: the tool and the prompt

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|4-8|11-14|17-20"}
memories = []   # lives outside every thread


@tool
def remember(fact: str) -> str:
    """Save a lasting fact about the user (name, classes, preferences, goals) for future conversations."""
    memories.append(fact)
    return "Saved."


BASE_PROMPT = (
    "You are a helpful tutor. When the user tells you something lasting about themselves, "
    "call the remember tool to save it."
)


def build_system_prompt(facts):
    if not facts:
        return BASE_PROMPT
    return BASE_PROMPT + "\n\nWhat you remember about the user:\n" + "\n".join(f"- {f}" for f in facts)
```

::: {.why}
**Write** = the tool. **Read** = `build_system_prompt`.
:::

## Stage 3: the chat loop

```{.python code-line-numbers="5-7|9-11|13"}
memory_agent = create_agent(MODEL, tools=[remember])
threads = {}


def chat(thread_id, text):
    history = threads.setdefault(thread_id, [])
    history.append(HumanMessage(text))

    # Read: rebuild the system prompt from memory every turn. It is NOT saved in the thread.
    system = SystemMessage(build_system_prompt(memories))
    result = memory_agent.invoke({"messages": [system] + history})

    history.extend(result["messages"][len(history) + 1:])   # +1 skips the system message
    return history[-1].text


print(chat("homework", "Hi, I'm Ana. I'm taking DS 250 and I prefer R over Python."))
print(chat("project", "Which language do I like?"))
```

::: {.why}
A brand-new thread knows Ana prefers R. `show(threads["homework"])` shows the tool call; `show(threads["project"])` doesn't.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Why not save the system message in the thread? Then every thread would carry a stale copy of the facts.
- In the project thread, the fact arrived through the prompt, not a tool call.
:::

## Stage 5: the code {.compact}

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|5-12|9|15-17|19-21"}
memories = {}   # user_id -> list of facts
threads = {}    # (user_id, thread_id) -> list of messages


def make_remember_tool(user_id):
    @tool
    def remember(fact: str) -> str:
        """Save a lasting fact about the user (name, classes, preferences, goals) for future conversations."""
        memories.setdefault(user_id, []).append(fact)
        return "Saved."

    return remember


def chat(user_id, thread_id, text):
    history = threads.setdefault((user_id, thread_id), [])
    history.append(HumanMessage(text))

    user_agent = create_agent(MODEL, tools=[make_remember_tool(user_id)])
    system = SystemMessage(build_system_prompt(memories.get(user_id, [])))
    result = user_agent.invoke({"messages": [system] + history})

    history.extend(result["messages"][len(history) + 1:])
    return history[-1].text
```

::: {.why}
`user_id` is in a **closure**, not the tool's signature. The model can't see it or change it.
:::

```{.python}
print(chat("ben", "homework", "I'm Ben. I'm a Python person, and I'm in DS 350."))
print(chat("ben", "chat-2", "What do you know about me?"))
print(chat("ana", "chat-2", "What do you know about me?"))

memories
```

Both use a thread called `"homework"`, and they don't collide. Each `chat-2` only knows its own user.
:::

## Framework version: tool and prompt {.compact}

```{.python code-line-numbers="9-11|14-19|17-18|22-26"}
import uuid
from dataclasses import dataclass

from langchain.agents.middleware import ModelRequest, dynamic_prompt
from langchain.tools import ToolRuntime
from langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore


@dataclass
class Context:
    user_id: str


@tool
def remember(fact: str, runtime: ToolRuntime[Context]) -> str:
    """Save a lasting fact about the user (name, classes, preferences, goals) for future conversations."""
    namespace = (runtime.context.user_id, "memories")
    runtime.store.put(namespace, str(uuid.uuid4()), {"fact": fact})
    return "Saved."


@dynamic_prompt
def prompt_with_memories(request: ModelRequest) -> str:
    namespace = (request.runtime.context.user_id, "memories")
    facts = [item.value["fact"] for item in request.runtime.store.search(namespace)]
    return build_system_prompt(facts)
```

::: {.why}
`runtime` is hidden from the model, just like our closure. The model only sees `fact`.
:::

## Framework version: the agent {.compact}

```{.python code-line-numbers="2-9|12-18"}
store = InMemoryStore()
fw_agent = create_agent(
    MODEL,
    tools=[remember],
    middleware=[prompt_with_memories],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
    store=store,
    context_schema=Context,
)


def fw_chat(user_id, thread_id, text):
    result = fw_agent.invoke(
        {"messages": [HumanMessage(text)]},
        {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}},
        context=Context(user_id=user_id),
    )
    return result["messages"][-1].text


print(fw_chat("ana", "ana-homework", "Hi, I'm Ana. I'm taking DS 250 and I prefer R over Python."))
print(fw_chat("ben", "ben-homework", "I'm Ben. I'm a Python person, and I'm in DS 350."))
print(fw_chat("ben", "ben-chat-2", "What do you know about me?"))
```

## What the framework doesn't do

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Ours]{.ct}
Threads keyed by `(user_id, thread_id)`. Ben **can't** open Ana's `"homework"`.
:::

::: {.card .warn}
[Checkpointer]{.ct}
Threads keyed by `thread_id` **alone**. Your app has to make sure a user only uses their own thread IDs.
:::
:::

::: {.why}
Here we prefix them (`"ana-homework"`). In a real app, **check who owns the thread** before calling the agent.
:::

<!-- ============================================================ -->
# Stage 6: One File per User {.center}

## The store is hard to see

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Invisible]{.ct}
Each fact is a separate row in RAM. Ana can't open it.
:::

::: {.card}
[Append-only]{.ct}
She changes her mind, and it keeps both "prefers R" **and** "switched to Python".
:::

::: {.card}
[Gone]{.ct}
It disappears when the Python process ends.
:::
:::

::: {.why .fragment style="text-align:center"}
Simpler: **one plain text file per user.** Readable, editable, and it lasts. (Claude Code's `CLAUDE.md` works the same way.)
:::

## The server enforces who's who

```{=html}
<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 1100 430" role="img" aria-label="Ana's agent gets a filesystem MCP server that can only see the folder /content/memories/ana. Write: the model calls write_file or edit_file through the server to change memory.md. Read: each turn, dynamic_prompt opens memory.md with plain Python and puts it in the system prompt. Ben's folder sits outside the server's reach.">

```

::: {.notes}
- Same two halves, split differently. Write: the model decides, so it gets the MCP write tools from 1.7. Read: the app's job. If reading were a tool, the model could forget to check.
- Isolation moved: Stage 5 baked user_id into the tool. Here the *server* can only see Ana's folder, so it can't write to Ben's no matter what anyone types.
:::

## Stage 6: one server per user {.compact}

```{.python code-line-numbers="13-15|17-20|21-22"}
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter

MEMORY_ROOT = "/content/memories"
WRITE_TOOLS = ("write_file", "edit_file")   # the only filesystem tools the model needs here
checkpointer = InMemorySaver()
file_agents = {}   # user_id -> agent


async def get_file_agent(user_id):
    if user_id in file_agents:
        return file_agents[user_id]

    folder = f"{MEMORY_ROOT}/{user_id}"
    os.makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
    path = f"{folder}/memory.md"

    # The server can only touch the folders listed at the end of args: this user's folder, nothing else.
    config = {"mcpServers": {
        "memory": {"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", folder]},
    }}
    async with MCPAdapter(config) as adapter:
        tools = [t for t in await adapter.list_tools() if t.name.endswith(WRITE_TOOLS)]
    ...
```

::: {.why}
`folder` at the end of `args` is the **only** place this server can touch.
:::

## Stage 6: read the file every turn {.compact}

```{.python code-line-numbers="2-4|5-10|12-14"}
    ...
    @dynamic_prompt
    def prompt_with_memory_file(request: ModelRequest) -> str:
        contents = open(path).read() if os.path.exists(path) else "(empty)"
        return (
            f"You are a helpful tutor. You keep one memory file about the user at {path}. "
            "When the user tells you something lasting about themselves, update that file. "
            "Keep it a short bulleted list, and edit existing lines instead of repeating them.\n\n"
            f"Current contents of {path}:\n{contents}"
        )

    agent = create_agent(MODEL, tools=tools, middleware=[prompt_with_memory_file], checkpointer=checkpointer)
    file_agents[user_id] = agent
    return agent
```

::: {.why}
**Read** is plain Python, not a tool. The model can't forget to check.
:::

## Stage 6: try it {.compact}

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-7|10-13"}
async def file_chat(user_id, thread_id, text):
    agent = await get_file_agent(user_id)
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [HumanMessage(text)]},
        {"configurable": {"thread_id": f"{user_id}-{thread_id}"}},
    )
    return result["messages"][-1].text


print(await file_chat("ana", "homework", "Hi, I'm Ana. I'm taking DS 250 and I prefer R over Python."))
print(await file_chat("ben", "homework", "I'm Ben. I'm a Python person, and I'm in DS 350."))
print(await file_chat("ana", "project", "Heads up: I've switched to Python this semester."))
print(await file_chat("ana", "chat-3", "What do you know about me?"))
```

::: {.why}
Open **Files → memories/**. Ana's file should say Python, **not both**. Edit it by hand, then ask again: the file *is* the memory.
:::

## What a file costs

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Every prompt]{.ct}
The whole file goes into every turn. As it grows, you pay for it, just like the thread in Stage 1.
:::

::: {.card}
[Two writers]{.ct}
Two chats editing at once can overwrite each other. A database handles that; one plain file doesn't.
:::

::: {.card}
[Colab resets]{.ct}
`/content` is wiped with the runtime. Point `MEMORY_ROOT` at Google Drive if you want it to last.
:::
:::

# Recap {.center}

## Memory is what the app sends

```{=html}
<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 1100 360" role="img" aria-label="Recap: the model is stateless. Short-term memory is the thread, a list of messages per thread ID. Long-term memory has two halves: write, where the model calls a tool, and read, where the app puts saved facts in the prompt every turn. Both are keyed by user, and identity comes from the app, not the model.">
  <rect class="dg-box" x="420" y="20" width="260" height="90" rx="14" stroke="#d2a8ff"/>
  <text class="dg-title" x="550" y="60" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:#d2a8ff">model</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="550" y="90" text-anchor="middle">stateless, always</text>

  <rect class="dg-box" x="30" y="150" width="320" height="170" rx="14" stroke="#58a6ff"/>
  <text class="dg-tag" x="50" y="178">SHORT-TERM</text>
  <text class="dg-title" x="50" y="215" style="fill:#79c0ff">threads</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="50" y="248">a list per thread ID</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="50" y="275">→ checkpointer</text>

  <rect class="dg-box" x="390" y="150" width="320" height="170" rx="14" stroke="#7ee787"/>
  <text class="dg-tag" x="410" y="178">LONG-TERM</text>
  <text class="dg-title" x="410" y="215" style="fill:#7ee787">write + read</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="410" y="248">model writes via a tool</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="410" y="275">app reads into the prompt</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="410" y="302">→ store / a file</text>

  <rect class="dg-box" x="750" y="150" width="320" height="170" rx="14" stroke="#ffa657"/>
  <text class="dg-tag" x="770" y="178">WHOSE?</text>
  <text class="dg-title" x="770" y="215" style="fill:#ffa657">keyed by user</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="770" y="248">identity from the app,</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="770" y="275">never from the model</text>
  <text class="dg-label" x="770" y="302">→ context / server scope</text>
</svg>
```

::: {.notes}
- One sentence to leave with: the model remembers nothing; memory is a decision about what the app sends.
- Ask: where would per-user memory help your Project 1 agent? Where would it be a liability?
:::
